entry.title: KTM24 v Rio Tinto Limited (Strike Out) [2026] FCA 1579
entry.content:
Rio Tinto applied to strike out parts of representative proceedings brought by the applicants alleging sexual harassment and sex discrimination in employment. The Federal Court struck out certain paragraphs of the pleadings for lack of material facts but granted leave to amend the group member definition and other pleadings, finding the applicants largely successful. Costs were awarded to the applicants as the overall successful party on the interlocutory applications.

Federal Court of Australia, 23 Oct 2026, [2026] FCA 1579

entry.title: Joyce v State of Queensland (Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation) [2026] QIRC 331
entry.content:
Michael Joyce appealed against an internal review decision confirming a management-initiated transfer from his substantive AO8 Regional Manager role to permanent alternative asset-management duties. The QIRC held the internal review decision was not fair and reasonable due to human rights and procedural compliance failures, allowed the appeal and returned him to his substantive position.

Key holding: A management-initiated transfer will not be fair and reasonable where the delegate does not hold a genuine two-way discussion with the employee before providing the written follow-up required by s 2.1.1 of the Transfer Guideline.

In my view, Mr Newman did not comply with s 2.1.1. That is because the section requires a 'discussion' with the employee to first occur before a written follow-up of the discussion is provided.

QIRC, 20 Oct 2026, [2026] QIRC 331

entry.title: XSLP and Telstra Corporation Limited (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2415
entry.content:
In XSLP and Telstra Corporation Limited (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2415, the Tribunal dealt with suppression orders made in XSLP’s compensation review and later discrimination/Federal Court proceedings. It varied a commercial-in-confidence order over Telstra documents by consent, continued an order protecting XSLP’s identity, and clarified that the parties could use evidence and reasons in Federal Court subject to those orders.

Key holding: Under the ART Act, the s 70 power to restrict publication or disclosure requires a mandatory s 71(2) weighing exercise, including all statutory considerations, before it can be exercised.

When considering whether to make an order under s 70, the weighing exercise required under s 71(2) is an essential prerequisite of the power to do so. In that exercise, the Tribunal must have regard to all the mandatory considerations in paragraphs 71(2)(a) to (e).

entry.title: Oss v State of Queensland (Queensland Health) [2026] QIRC 297
entry.content:
A part-time registered nurse appealed a Queensland Health disciplinary finding that substantiated conduct allegations against her, and also sought suppression and de-identification of her identity. The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission dismissed the suppression application, applying open justice principles, and confirmed the disciplinary finding decision as fair and reasonable. The Commission noted that any proposed disciplinary action (including possible termination) remained a separate matter outside the scope of the appeal.

QIRC, 16 Sep 2026, [2026] QIRC 297

entry.title: Dryden v State of Queensland (Queensland Health) [2026] QIRC 265
entry.content:
A registered nurse employed by Queensland Health resigned after misconduct findings were made against her. A post-separation disciplinary declaration was made that she would have been terminated had she remained employed. She appealed, but the Commission found the underlying disciplinary findings were out of time (statute barred) and that the disciplinary declaration was fair and reasonable, confirming it.

QIRC, 25 Aug 2026, [2026] QIRC 265

entry.title: Heywood v State of Queensland (Department of Education) [2026] QIRC 261
entry.content:
The appellant, a teacher, appealed against a disciplinary finding that she engaged in inappropriate conduct toward students and against the reprimand imposed. The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission found the alleged conduct occurred as alleged and that both the finding and the reprimand were fair, reasonable and proportionate, considering mitigating factors such as her mental health and unblemished record.

entry.title: Pariyar v Basnet as Trustee for the Rojal and Reshma Family Trust &Ors (No. 2) [2026] QIRC 259
entry.content:

The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission found the sexual harassment and discrimination proven and awarded $255,750 in compensation, including aggravated damages, but declined to order an apology or anti-discrimination programs.

entry.title: Leyshon v State of Queensland (Queensland Health) [2026] QIRC 241
entry.content:
Ms Leyshon, an Operational Services Officer with Queensland Health, appealed a directive decision dated 10 March 2026 but filed her appeal notice on 21 April 2026, outside the 21-day statutory timeframe. She sought an extension of time, blaming confusion about which union representative could assist her. The Commission refused the extension, finding the delay significant and the explanation unreasonable, and dismissed the appeal for want of jurisdiction.

QIRC, 5 Aug 2026, [2026] QIRC 241

entry.title: Mills v State of Queensland (Department of Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation) [2026] QIRC 206
entry.content:
A Queensland public sector employee appealed an internal review decision confirming a direction to attend an Independent Medical Examination. The Commission considered only whether the decision complied with s103 of the Public Sector Act 2022 (Qld), finding the chief executive was reasonably satisfied the employee was absent from duty and reasonably suspected the absence was caused by mental illness, and that the decision was fair and reasonable. The decision appealed against was confirmed.

QIRC, 19 Jun 2026, [2026] QIRC 206

entry.title: Mr Joseph Akot v Australian Health Practitioner Regulatory Agency [2025] FWC 3745
entry.content:
Mr Akot was appointed to AHPRA's Community Advisory Council on a fixed-term basis and received sitting fees for attending meetings. After his membership was terminated following an investigation, he applied for an unfair dismissal remedy. The Commission found that, on the totality of the relationship, he was not an employee within the meaning of ss 15 and 15AA, and dismissed the application for lack of jurisdiction.

Fair Work Commission, 5 Dec 2025, [2025] FWC 3745

entry.title: Ms Tracey-Anne Kathleen Rising v Barto Gold Mining Pty Ltd & Yuxin Holdings Pty Limited [2025] FWC 1405
entry.content:
The applicant lodged a general protections application 21 days after her alleged dismissal but sought an extension of time. The Fair Work Commission found that the circumstances were not exceptional, weighing the reason for delay and merits against an extension, and therefore dismissed the application. The applicant's claim that she was dismissed was also contested on jurisdictional grounds.

Fair Work Commission, 23 May 2025, [2025] FWC 1405
